## What you shared, in brief

You described a pattern that the texts name: Ārta-dhyāna (sorrowful dwelling), in the Jain texts. Each is shown below with your own words and the texts' description.

## Patterns the texts describe

### Ārta-dhyāna (sorrowful dwelling) (Jain)

- Your words: “i want to go straight back to it”
- Why this fits: You wrote "i want to go straight back to it"; the texts describe this as the mind fixed on getting back what is pleasant and lost (ts 9.31).
- How sure: low
- Texts: Tattvārthasūtra 9.31

## The Vedic and yogic reading

- The Vedic and yogic texts have their own account of a pattern like the one above: Daurmanasya (dejection) (a partial match for Ārta-dhyāna (sorrowful dwelling)). Dejection is agitation of the mind from the thwarting of a wish (icchā-vighāta). Your words were matched to Ārta-dhyāna (sorrowful dwelling), not to this; it is shown so that both readings are in view. _(Yogabhāṣya (Vyāsa's commentary on the Yoga Sūtra) 1.31; Yoga Sūtra of Patañjali 1.31)_

## The ascetic reading (Buddhist and Jain)

- Your words “i want to go straight back to it” fit only loosely what the Jain texts call Ārta-dhyāna (sorrowful dwelling). Meditation (dhyāna) is of four kinds: sorrowful (ārta), cruel (raudra), virtuous (dharmya) and pure (śukla) (TS 9.28); the last two are causes of liberation (TS 9.29). _(Tattvārthasūtra 9.28; Tattvārthasūtra 9.29)_

## How the two readings fit together

- For what you wrote, “i want to go straight back to it”: Each names a sinking, sorrowful turn of mind. Vyāsa: dejection (daurmanasya) is a disturbance of the mind through the frustration of a wish, and it accompanies distraction (YS 1.31; YB 1.31). Gītā: Arjuna is overcome by pity and despairing (viṣīdan), his mind bewildered about dharma (BhG 1.28, 2.1, 2.7). TS: sorrowful dwelling (ārta-dhyāna) dwells on removing the disagreeable, on keeping the agreeable, on pain, and on longing for future enjoyment (TS 9.30–33). MN 10 declares the four establishments of mindfulness a path to the ending of pain and displeasure (dukkha-domanassa) (MN 10:2). Under the one-truth principle, they describe it from different standpoints: the match is a partial match, not an identity. _(standpoint; Yoga Sūtra of Patañjali 1.31; Yogabhāṣya (Vyāsa's commentary on the Yoga Sūtra) 1.31; Bhagavad Gītā 1.28; Bhagavad Gītā 2.1; Bhagavad Gītā 2.7; Tattvārthasūtra 9.30; Tattvārthasūtra 9.31; Tattvārthasūtra 9.32; Tattvārthasūtra 9.33; Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta mn10:2)_
- Where they differ: For what you wrote, “i want to go straight back to it”: (1) Daurmanasya in YS is a companion of distraction: it occurs in a distracted mind and is absent in a concentrated one (YB 1.31). (2) Arjuna's viṣāda is a crisis about dharma, and it becomes the occasion of the whole teaching (BhG 2.7). (3) Jain ārta-dhyāna is a kind of meditation (dhyāna), the inauspicious sorrowful one of four (TS 9.28): a sustained fixing of the mind, not a passing mood. This row describes states the texts name. It is not a finding about any person, and it makes no health claim. _(Yoga Sūtra of Patañjali 1.31; Yogabhāṣya (Vyāsa's commentary on the Yoga Sūtra) 1.31; Bhagavad Gītā 2.7; Tattvārthasūtra 9.28)_

## A gentle practice pathway

### The reflections (anuprekṣā, TS 9.7)

You wrote “i want to go straight back to it”. This reading suggests the practice below for what the texts call Ārta-dhyāna (sorrowful dwelling). The practice comes from the texts cited with it; the pairing with this pattern is this reading's, not theirs.

1. Sit comfortably.
2. Reflect repeatedly on impermanence (anitya), as the sūtra names it (TS 9.7).
3. Reflect on aloneness (ekatva) and on otherness (anyatva), as the sūtra names them (TS 9.7).
4. Reflect on the rarity of enlightenment (bodhi-durlabha) (TS 9.7).
5. Reflect on the well-taught nature of dharma (dharma-svākhyātatva) (TS 9.7).
6. Close gently.

Length: 5–10 minutes, 1 time(s) a day (product default for a beginner; the text gives no length).

**The texts' caution:** Nearest general caution in the Tattvārtha (the sūtra gives none for this practice): reflection must not turn into sorrowful brooding (ārta-dhyāna), which the sūtra defines as dwelling on removing the disagreeable, keeping the agreeable, on pain, and hankering for future enjoyment (nidāna). _(Tattvārthasūtra 9.30; Tattvārthasūtra 9.31; Tattvārthasūtra 9.32; Tattvārthasūtra 9.33)_

_Texts: Tattvārthasūtra 9.7; Tattvārthasūtra 9.2_

## What you shared, in brief

You described a pattern that the texts name: Cañcala manas (the restless mind), in the Vedic/yogic texts. Each is shown below with your own words and the texts' description.

## Patterns the texts describe

### Cañcala manas (the restless mind) (Vedic/yogic)

- Your words: “At night my mind runs like a sewing machine”; “When I sit for my evening prayer the mind is jumping everywhere”
- Why this fits: You wrote "At night my mind runs like a sewing machine"; the texts describe this as the mind moving off wherever it will, restless and unsteady (bhg 6.26, 6.34).
- How sure: moderate
- Texts: Bhagavad Gītā 6.26; Bhagavad Gītā 6.34

## The Vedic and yogic reading

- Your words “At night my mind runs like a sewing machine” may fit what the Vedic and yogic texts call Cañcala manas (the restless mind). Arjuna: the mind is restless, turbulent, strong and obstinate; I think it as hard to hold as the wind (BhG 6.34). Kṛṣṇa: no doubt the mind is hard to hold and moving, but it is held by practice and dispassion (6.35). The turbulent senses carry off by force the mind even of a wise man who strives (2.60); the mind that follows the roving senses carries off understanding as the wind a ship on the water (2.67). _(Bhagavad Gītā 2.60; Bhagavad Gītā 2.67; Bhagavad Gītā 6.34; Bhagavad Gītā 6.35)_

## The ascetic reading (Buddhist and Jain)

- The Buddhist texts have their own account of a pattern like the one above: Uddhacca-kukkucca (restlessness and remorse) (a partial match for Cañcala manas (the restless mind)). Contemplating dhammas as the five hindrances: when restlessness and remorse is present in him the monk knows 'there is restlessness and remorse in me'; when absent, 'there is no restlessness and remorse in me'; he knows how the unarisen restlessness and remorse arises, how the arisen restlessness and remorse is abandoned, and how the abandoned restlessness and remorse does not arise again. Your words were matched to Cañcala manas (the restless mind), not to this; it is shown so that both readings are in view. _(Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta dn22:13; Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta mn10:36)_

## How the two readings fit together

- For what you wrote, “At night my mind runs like a sewing machine”: Each names a mind that will not stay. Gītā: the mind is restless, turbulent, strong and obstinate, as hard to restrain as the wind (BhG 6.34). It is held by practice and dispassion (BhG 6.35), and wherever it wanders it is to be brought back (BhG 6.26). Vyāsa: samādhi is a property of the mind at every level, and one of its grounds is the distracted (vikṣipta) (YB 1.1). Suttas: restlessness and remorse (uddhacca-kukkucca) is a hindrance known as present or absent (MN 10:36), and a scattered (vikkhitta) mind is known as scattered (MN 10:34). Under the one-truth principle, they describe it from different standpoints: the match is a partial match, not an identity. _(standpoint; Bhagavad Gītā 6.34; Bhagavad Gītā 6.35; Bhagavad Gītā 6.26; Yogabhāṣya (Vyāsa's commentary on the Yoga Sūtra) 1.1; Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta mn10:36; Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta mn10:34)_
- Where they differ: For what you wrote, “At night my mind runs like a sewing machine”: (1) Vyāsa's distracted mind is one ground in a scale of grounds of mind (YB 1.1). MN 10 only names the scattered mind as something to be known, with no scale (MN 10:34). (2) The hindrance joins restlessness and remorse (kukkucca) into one (MN 10:36). The Gītā passage speaks of restlessness alone. (3) The Gītā names the remedy, practice and dispassion (BhG 6.35). MN 10's approach in this passage is to know the hindrance as present, arising and abandoned (MN 10:36). (4) The Visuddhimagga defines restlessness by its mark of non-calming (Vism XIV). It counts restlessness among the fetters that remain until the arahat path (Vism XXII), a depth that the Gītā and Vyāsa passages do not grade. _(Bhagavad Gītā 6.35; Yogabhāṣya (Vyāsa's commentary on the Yoga Sūtra) 1.1; Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta mn10:36; Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta mn10:34; Visuddhimagga 14.p469; Visuddhimagga 22.p682)_

## A gentle practice pathway

### Practice and dispassion (abhyāsa, vairāgya, BhG 6.35)

You wrote “At night my mind runs like a sewing machine”. This reading suggests the practice below for what the texts call Cañcala manas (the restless mind). The same passage that describes it (Bhagavad Gītā 6.26; Bhagavad Gītā 6.34; Bhagavad Gītā 6.35) also gives this practice.

1. Sit on a firm seat in a clean place, neither too high nor too low (BhG 6.11), body, head and neck in line and still (6.13).
2. Practice (abhyāsa): wherever the restless mind wanders off, restrain it from there and bring it back (6.26).
3. Dispassion (vairāgya): recall that enjoyments born of contact have a beginning and an end and are wombs of sorrow; the wise one does not delight in them (5.22).
4. Come to rest little by little (śanaiḥ śanaiḥ), not all at once (6.25).
5. Close gently.

Length: 5–10 minutes, 1 time(s) a day (product default for a beginner; the text gives no length).

**The texts' caution:** Moderation: yoga is not for one who eats too much, nor for one who does not eat at all, nor for one who sleeps too much or keeps always awake; it is for one measured in food, recreation, effort, sleep and waking. _(Bhagavad Gītā 6.16; Bhagavad Gītā 6.17)_

**The texts' caution:** The Gītā asks that yoga be practised with resolve and with an undejected mind (anirviṇṇa-cetas). _(Bhagavad Gītā 6.23)_

**The texts' caution:** The Gītā grants that the mind is hard to restrain; it is held by practice and dispassion (6.35), and yoga can be attained by one who strives through the right means (6.36). _(Bhagavad Gītā 6.35; Bhagavad Gītā 6.36)_
